securityInformation.title: Bypassing enforce mountable secrets policy imposed by the ServiceAccount admission plugin
securityInformation.description:
A security issue was discovered in Kubernetes where users may be able to launch containers that bypass the mountable secrets policy enforced by the ServiceAccount admission plugin when using ephemeral containers. The policy ensures pods running with a service account may only reference secrets specified in the service account's secrets field. Kubernetes clusters are only affected if the ServiceAccount admission plugin and the `kubernetes.io/enforce-mountable-secrets` annotation are used together with ephemeral containers.

**Note**: This only impacts the cluster if the ServiceAccount admission plugin is used (most cluster should have this on by default as recommended in https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/admission-controllers/#serviceaccount), the `kubernetes.io/enforce-mountable-secrets` annotation is used by a service account (this annotation is not added by default), and Pods are using ephemeral containers.

securityInformation.title: Unauthorized read of Custom Resources
securityInformation.description: A security issue was discovered in Kubernetes where users authorized to list or watch one type of namespaced custom resource cluster-wide can read custom resources of a different type in the same API group they are not authorized to read.

securityInformation.title: Node address isn't always verified when proxying
securityInformation.description:
A security issue was discovered in Kubernetes where users may have access to secure endpoints in the control plane network. Kubernetes clusters are only affected if an untrusted user can to modify Node objects and send requests proxying through them.

Kubernetes supports node proxying, which allows clients of kube-apiserver to access endpoints of a Kubelet to establish connections to Pods, retrieve container logs, and more. While Kubernetes already validates the proxying address for Nodes, a bug in kube-apiserver made it possible to bypass this validation. Bypassing this validation could allow authenticated requests destined for Nodes to be redirected to the API Server through its private network.

The merged fix enforces validation against the proxying address for a Node. In some cases, the fix can break clients that depend on the `nodes/proxy` subresource, specifically if a kubelet advertises a localhost or link-local address to the Kubernetes control plane. Configuring an egress proxy for egress to the cluster network can also mitigate this vulnerability.

securityInformation.title: Aggregated API server can cause clients to be redirected (SSRF)
securityInformation.description:
A security issue was discovered in kube-apiserver that could allow an attacker controlled aggregated API server to redirect client traffic to any URL.  This could lead to the client performing unexpected actions as well as leaking the client's credentials to third parties. 

There is no mitigation from this issue.  Cluster admins should take care to secure aggregated API servers and should not grant access to mutate `APIService`s to untrusted parties.

#### How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible):

enrichment.problem: During node startup, kubelet reported a node ready status before the node allocatable *ephemeral-storage* value was populated. The scheduler consequently thought the node lacked sufficient storage, causing pod admission failures (e.g., etcd, kube-apiserver) and kubeadm join operations on new control‑plane nodes to fail or crash.
enrichment.affected: New nodes (especially control‑plane nodes) joining a cluster via kubeadm, and any pods that require ephemeral‑storage during node startup.
enrichment.fix: Kubelet now blocks the transition to Ready until the node's allocatable ephemeral‑storage information is obtained. The code adds a wait for the storage data during node status setting, ensuring the node reports correct resource capacity before it can be used for scheduling.
enrichment.impact: Cluster bootstrap and control‑plane node joins become reliable even when the root filesystem has ample space. Pods are no longer incorrectly rejected for lacking ephemeral storage, preventing CrashLoopBackOff and join failures.

bugOrRegression.description: Fix for volume reconstruction of CSI ephemeral volumes
bugOrRegression.author: dobsonj

issueContext.title: CSI volume reconstruction does not work for ephemeral volumes
issueContext.body:
When a pod is marked as deleted while kubelet is down / being restarted, newly started kubelet does not clean up  CSI filesystem volumes of the pod.

Newly started kubelet tries to reconstruct the volume using CSI's `ConstructVolumeSpec` function. This part looks working, CSI volume plugin loads its json file.

But then VolumeManager checks if the volume is still mounted in `/var/lib/kubelet/pods/9440e7e5-d454-4555-84b7-d72e43ec4b3a/volumes/kubernetes.io~csi/pvc-45640a32-4ba3-4a7d-ad4b-087281f1460d/mount` directory.

There are two issues:

1. CSI does not require volumes to be presented as mounts. They can be just directories with files on them. This will be case of the most of in-line volumes.

2. ~~Even if the CSI driver used mount, kubelet mounts it into `/var/lib/kubelet/pods/9440e7e5-d454-4555-84b7-d72e43ec4b3a/volumes/kubernetes.io~csi/pvc-45640a32-4ba3-4a7d-ad4b-087281f1460d/mount`. Checking of `/var/lib/kubelet/pods/9440e7e5-d454-4555-84b7-d72e43ec4b3a/volumes/kubernetes.io~csi/pvc-45640a32-4ba3-4a7d-ad4b-087281f1460d` does not make sense.~~
  Kubelet checks the right directory given by `GetPath()`

enrichment.problem: When a pod is deleted while the kubelet is down, the restarted kubelet fails to clean up CSI filesystem (ephemeral) volumes because it incorrectly checks for a mount point. CSI drivers may expose volumes as plain directories, so the mount check prevents proper reconstruction and cleanup.
enrichment.affected: Workloads with CSI ephemeral (inline) volumes that are deleted while the kubelet is down or being restarted.

issueContext.title: CronJob controller V2: breaks "@every [interval]" jobs
issueContext.body:
#### What happened:

In K8s 1.21, CronJobs with a `.spec.schedule` with a value containing something like `@every 6h` are inconsistently scheduled, and the CronJob's `.status.lastScheduleTime` field does not match reality.

For example, I have a CronJob configured as above. It runs every 6 hours as long as the kube-controller-manager pod isn't restarted, but the `.status.lastScheduleTime` is currently some 45 minutes _before_ the Job's `.spec.metadata.creationTimestamp`. The kube-controller-manager's logs correctly show the job is created corresponding with the Job's creationTimestamp, and the CronJob's lastScheduleTime appears to be updated at the same time, but with a time stamp in the past.

In K8s 1.20 the behaviour was as expected, and the lastScheduleTime closely (possibly even exactly) matched the Job's creationTimestamp.

#### What you expected to happen:

Jobs created from CronJobs should be consistently created every 6 hours (for `@every 6h`), and the `.status.lastScheduleTime` should closely follow the last Job's `.spec.metadata.creationTimestamp` field.

#### How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible):

I see consistent behaviour on multiple clusters running 1.21 (in AWS EKS and built using Rancher RKE2), but I haven't tried with timestamps shorter than 6 hours. This is easily reproducible with `@every 6h` timestamps, however.

#### Anything else we need to know?:

The `@every` syntax is not documented in the Kubernetes [CronJob documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/cron-jobs/), though that mostly points at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cron) for the schedule format. However, the `@every` syntax works and is documented in [`vendor/github.com/robfig/cron/v3/doc.go`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/vendor/github.com/robfig/cron/v3/doc.go) and at https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/robfig/cron.

The implementation for `@every` is at: https://github.com/kubern

enrichment.problem: CronJob controller v2 mishandles `@every` interval schedules, causing jobs to be created at the correct times but the CronJob's `.status.lastScheduleTime` is set to a past timestamp, leading to inconsistent scheduling information and potential confusion for users.
enrichment.affected: Clusters running CronJobs with `@every` interval schedules (e.g., `@every 6h`). The CronJob controller in the kube‑controller‑manager is affected.
enrichment.fix: The controller manager's CronJob scheduling logic was updated to correctly compute the next run time for `@every` schedules and to set `.status.lastScheduleTime` to match the actual Job creation timestamp.
enrichment.impact: CronJobs that use the `@every` syntax now schedule reliably and report accurate status, preventing missed runs or misleading status information for workloads that depend on periodic execution.

issueContext.title: Job tracking might leave pods with finalizers when backoff limit is reached
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

A job reached it's backoff limit and pods were left with finalizers.

The `.status.uncountedTerminatedPods` was left empty.

### What did you expect to happen?

The pods to not have a finalizer

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

We don't have a low scale repro. But we observe this:

```
spec:
  backoffLimit: 0
  completionMode: Indexed
  completions: 5000
  parallelism: 5000
status:
  completedIndexes: 0-4003,4005
  conditions:
  - lastProbeTime: "2022-04-14T14:09:23Z"
    lastTransitionTime: "2022-04-14T14:09:23Z"
    message: Job has reached the specified backoff limit
    reason: BackoffLimitExceeded
    status: "True"
    type: Failed
  failed: 1
  startTime: "2022-04-14T13:57:54Z"
  succeeded: 4005
  uncountedTerminatedPods: {}
```

1 Pod failed, potentially 4004. What happened to 4006 and beyond? The job controller creates pods in batches of 500, so it looks like the job was declared finished before observing all the pods that it created.
I confirmed from the kcm logs that the pod was created:

```
"Event occurred" object="default/job-foo" kind="Job" apiVersion="batch/v1" type="Normal" reason="SuccessfulCreate" message="Created pod: job-foo-4006-zjrqh"
```

### Anything else we need to know?

This cluster doesn't have the patch #109020. However, the job still exists, so it doesn't sound like it's the same bug.

enrichment.affected: Users running batch Jobs (especially indexed/completionMode=Indexed) that reach backoff limits or have many parallel pods. The bug caused leftover pod finalizers and premature Job completion.

issueContext.title: [scale] node state changes causes excessive LB re-configurations
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

There is scale bug related to the cloud-controller-manager, namely: when a cluster reaches a state where the relation between the amount of LBs and cluster nodes reaches an almost equal amount (i.e: a many-to-many relation between LBs and nodes) the amount of cloud API calls performed by the CCM to sync LBs can become overwhelming for the cloud provider. This can (among other things) lead to:

1. an excessive amount of cloud API calls for the LB re-configurations
2. rate limiting by the cloud provider as an effect of 1.
3. or worse: a non-trivial amount of time to sync all services in the cluster, leading to desynchronized LBs.

An example of problem 3. is: imagine we have 200 LBs and 500 nodes, on clusters at such scale, the amount of events processed by the CCM for transitioning node state can become important. The current implementation of the CCM will resync all 200 LB services for any node which has a transitioning state - as to keep the LBs' configured backends in sync with the state of the cluster. It has been observed that on clusters at that scale, the cloud provider can take up to hours to process a full resync for all services. A scenario such as the below is hence not improbable (and actually quite likely):

1. Node25 transitions from Ready -> NotReady
[All LB services are synced - time taken for this might be long]
2. Service1's LB which only has an endpoint on Node25 gets Node25 removed from its list of backend
3. Node25 transitions from NotReady -> Ready again, cancelling the scheduled eviction for the endpoint hosted on Node25 for Service1
4. CCM is still processing the updated caused by 1. and clients connecting to the LB of Service1 continues experiencing connectivity issues, even though Node25 now is in a Ready state.
[Eventually - once the CCM enters its second reconciliation loop caused by 3.]
5. The LB for Service1 gets Node25 added to its list of backend again and connectivity is again achieved by clients.

enrichment.problem: When a node’s readiness transitions (Ready ↔ NotReady), the service controller in cloud‑controller‑manager re‑syncs every LoadBalancer service with externalTrafficPolicy=Local. At scale (many LBs and nodes) this triggers a flood of cloud API calls, causing rate‑limiting, long sync times, and service downtime.
enrichment.affected: Clusters that run services with externalTrafficPolicy=Local and have many LoadBalancer services, especially large clusters where node state changes are frequent.
enrichment.fix: The service controller now skips resyncs for nodes that are in a transitioning state for services with externalTrafficPolicy=Local. LoadBalancers will rely solely on the healthCheckNodePort probe to decide whether a node should receive traffic, eliminating unnecessary LB re‑configurations.
enrichment.impact: Reduces cloud provider API traffic, prevents rate‑limiting and long LB sync periods, and eliminates brief service outages when nodes flap, improving reliability for services using externalTrafficPolicy=Local.

issueContext.title: Enabling external CCM causes Node.Addresses to flap
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

I am reproducing this in OpenShift using the OpenStack cloud provider, but nothing here is specific to either OpenShift or OpenStack.

When migrating a cluster which uses in-tree cloud provider to use external cloud-provider, we use the following process:

1. Disable cloud controllers in KCM
2. Deploy CCM
3. Redeploy kubelets with --cloud-provider=external

Between steps 1&2 the node-lifecycle, routes, and service controllers are not running anywhere, but this situation isn't unsafe for the cluster and we can keep it short.

Between steps 2&3 is more interesting. The node controller is running in CCM, and the kubelets are running with --cloud-provider=openstack (or whatever, just not external). The main loop of node-controller will ignore a newly created node because [it won't have the external cloud provider taint](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/1234d061c0bdc53b41bc7c12881bbaa7af084e55/staging/src/k8s.io/cloud-provider/controllers/node/node_controller.go#L394-L399). However, the [UpdateNodeStatus()](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/1234d061c0bdc53b41bc7c12881bbaa7af084e55/staging/src/k8s.io/cloud-provider/controllers/node/node_controller.go#L166) loop does not have a similar exclusion.

[Kubelet also manages Node.Addresses](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/1234d061c0bdc53b41bc7c12881bbaa7af084e55/pkg/kubelet/nodestatus/setters.go#L62-L209). Note that we shortcut if the kubelet is using an external cloud provider, but not if we don't. So between steps 2&3 both kubelet and CCM's node controller are managing Node.Addresses. If the legacy cloud provider and external CCM don't return the same list of NodeAddresses this causes flapping.

Running OpenShift on OpenStack we have 2 problems. Firstly, our legacy cloud provider and external CCM produce different lists. We don't think this would be a problem in practise, except for the second problem.

Kubelet adds the `alpha.kubernetes.io/provided-n

enrichment.problem: The alpha.kubernetes.io/provided-node-ip annotation was only added when kubelet was started with --cloud-provider=external. When using in-tree cloud providers (or during migration to external CCM), the annotation was missing, causing the node controller to see inconsistent Node.Status.Addresses and leading to address flapping and node readiness issues.
enrichment.affected: Clusters that use in-tree cloud providers or are migrating to an external cloud controller manager experienced node address flapping and node controller mis‑recognition.
enrichment.fix: Kubelet now adds the provided-node-ip annotation on startup whenever any --cloud-provider flag is set, including deprecated in-tree providers, ensuring the annotation is always present regardless of the provider type.
enrichment.impact: Prevents node address churn during cloud‑provider migrations and ensures consistent node status reporting for clusters using in-tree providers, improving stability and reducing downtime.

    return "resource"

  if requestInfo.Namespace != "" {

```

issueContext.title: Kubelet reports Ready=true for pod and containers conditions during kubelet level evictions
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

In 1.22+, when kubelet evicts a pod, it updates the pod status to api-server marking the pod phase as failed / succeeded. However, the kubelet continues to report Ready=true pod condition until the all of the containers are fully terminated by the container runtime. 

As a result, since the pod is still considered ready, external controllers (e.g. the endpoint controller), utilize the pod ready condition and will continue to send traffic to these pods marked in terminal phase. These pods are often not ready to serve traffic since they are in progress of being shutdown. 

This is regression from prior to 1.22, since prior to 1.22, kubelet did not send any pod/container conditions to the api-server for evicted pods. 

xref: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/105358#issuecomment-932470027 for difference between kubelet status for evicted pods before and after 1.22

One of the areas where this issue manifests is with Kubelet graceful shutdown. In 1.22+, if a pod takes a long time to shutdown, during the entire shutdown process the kubelet will report Ready=true condition, and traffic will be sent to the pod. 

Additionally, If the node is shutdown before the pod fully terminates, the pod will be stuck in this state where Phase=Failed, but Ready=true. As a result, the pod will be seen incorrectly as ready by services and will be sent traffic (which the pod will likely be unable to handle due to either the pod being in progress of terminating or the node already being shutdown). 

I suspect this is issue not only for graceful shutdown, but for any type of kubelet initiated eviction. 

### What did you expect to happen?

Kubelet should maintain the same behavior as prior to 1.22. Kubelet should report Ready=false condition at the same time as marking Phase=Failed for evicted pods. Having pods in terminal phases (i.e. Failed / Succeeded), but Ready=true should not be a possible status update from kubelet to api-server.

enrichment.problem: Kubelet could send pod status updates where the pod phase is terminal (Failed or Succeeded) but the Ready condition remains true, causing services and endpoint controllers to consider the pod ready and route traffic to pods that are being terminated or have been evicted.

issueContext.title: activeDeadlineSeconds not working correctly for Jobs in 1.24.0
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

Prior to 1.24.0 setting `spec.adctiveDeadlineSeconds` in a Job object (`batch/v1`) would kill the Job and Pods if they ran longer than the integer specified. I tested today with 1.24.0 and it's not working. The Job defined below (for testing) should be killed 10 seconds, but isn't. It's actually being terminated after about 55 seconds.

```
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: test
spec:
  activeDeadlineSeconds: 10
  ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 120
  completions: 5
  parallelism: 1
  backoffLimit: 4
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
      - name: ctr
        image: alpine:latest
        command: ['sh', '-c', 'echo "TEST" && sleep 60']
```

### What did you expect to happen?

The Job to be killed after 10 seconds as per `activeDeadlineSeconds: 10`. It's worked like this in 1.23.x.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

On a cluster running 1.24.0 with the following YAML file called `job.yml`.

**job.yml**
```
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: test
spec:
  activeDeadlineSeconds: 10
  ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 120
  completions: 5
  parallelism: 1
  backoffLimit: 4
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
      - name: ctr
        image: alpine:latest
        command: ['sh', '-c', 'echo "TEST" && sleep 60']
```

Create the Job.
`kubectl apply -f job.yml`

On Kubernetes clusters earlier than 1.24.0 it would fail after 10 seconds and the following command should show `Warning  DeadlineExceeded  Xs     job-controller  Job was active longer than specified deadline` in the events 10 seconds after the **Pod** is created.

`kubectl describe job test`

```
<SNIP>
Events:
  Type     Reason            Age   From            Message
  ----     ------            ----  ----            -------
  Normal   SuccessfulCreate  16s   job-controller  Created pod: ckad1-kk6jt
  Normal   SuccessfulDelete

enrichment.problem: In Kubernetes 1.24 the job controller failed to enforce the `spec.activeDeadlineSeconds` field for Job objects, allowing pods to run far beyond the configured deadline.
enrichment.affected: Clusters running 1.24.0+ where users create batch/v1 Job resources with `activeDeadlineSeconds` set. Any workload relying on deadline enforcement was impacted.
enrichment.fix: The job controller logic was corrected so that it now monitors and terminates Jobs and their Pods once the active deadline is reached, restoring the behavior present in previous releases.
enrichment.impact: Jobs with `activeDeadlineSeconds` now terminate as expected, preventing unnecessary resource consumption and ensuring that TTL and cleanup semantics work reliably.

issueContext.title: `--chunk-size` with selector returns missing result, so `describe node` / `drain` could be works wrong
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

`kubectl get` has `--chunk-size=500` by default, and since 1.22 `describe` `drain` has the same.   
 https://github.com/kubernetes/kubectl/issues/1028

They seem to return wrong results in certain situations combined with `--selector` / `--field-selector`.

And `kubectl describe node` / `kubectl drain` also use `--field-selector=spec.nodeName=NODE`, so they also don't work correctly.  
`describe node` outputs partial list of pods on the node, `drain` doesn't evict some of the pods.

To make it work correctly, I had to specify `--chunk-size=0`


### What did you expect to happen?

`get` `describe` `drain` works correctly with any `chunk-size`, since it's just a performance optimizing parameter.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

I can't provide an actual concrete example (no `--chunk-size` = default `chunk-size=500`), but instead I show how to reproduce it with a smaller `chunk-size`

I believe that the same problem occurs with `chunk-size=500`

----

create two deployments.

```
$ kubectl create deployment hello-server --image=us-docker.pkg.dev/google-samples/containers/gke/hello-app:1.0 --replicas=5
$ kubectl create deployment another-server --image=us-docker.pkg.dev/google-samples/containers/gke/hello-app:1.0 --replicas=5
```

 there are 5 pods in each.

```

another-server-65f84969d6-x6vl5   1/1     Running   0          4s

hello-server-7bb955f957-dsdpj     1/1     Running   0          58s

hello-server

enrichment.problem: When `kubectl` commands (e.g., get, describe node, drain) were run with both `--chunk-size` (default 500) and a `--selector` or `--field-selector`, the client returned an incorrect result length, causing missing pods in the output and incomplete eviction during drain.
enrichment.affected: Any administrator or automation that uses `kubectl` with `--chunk-size` together with `--selector`/`--field-selector`, especially when describing nodes or draining them.
enrichment.fix: The kubectl client was updated to correctly handle pagination when a selector is provided, ensuring the full set of matching resources is returned regardless of the chunk size.
enrichment.impact: Users no longer need to set `--chunk-size=0` as a workaround; `kubectl get`, `describe node`, and `drain` now list all matching pods and evict them correctly, improving reliability of day‑to‑day cluster operations.

issueContext.title: Volumes are detached while they're still mounted on a node
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

A/D controller tries to detach volumes that are still mounted after 6 minutes. The conditions to trigger the detach are: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/9a75e7b0fd1b567f774a3373be640e19b33e7ef1/pkg/volume/util/util.go#L387

I.e. all containers are finished. But that does not guarantee that volumes are unmounted. When a CSI driver can't unmount a volume for 6 minutes, the volume is force detached by A/D controller, corrupting the volume and leaving volume mounts on the node in a bad state. Note that the node is perfectly healthy, it just can't unmount a volume from whatever reason.

### What did you expect to happen?

A/D controller detaches volumes after a Pod is deleted from the API server, i.e. the volumes are unmounted or someone force-deleted the pods.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Very artificial reproducer:

1. Run a Pod with an attachable CSI volume.
2. On the node, make the volume mount busy, e.g.:
    ```
    cd /var/lib/kubelet/pods/f377d5c5-1463-4d55-ad80-51a3e12e2251/volumes/kubernetes.io~csi/pvc-2443e93b-380f-4015-bda9-3a71ddc6e737/mount
    ```
    Every unmount of the volume fails and kubelet/the CSI driver periodically retry.
3. Delete the pod
4. After 6 minutes, see the volume is detached without unmounting first.

KCM logs:
```
W1129 10:46:55.629375    9230 reconciler.go:224] attacherDetacher.DetachVolume started for volume "pvc-2443e93b-380f-4015-bda9-3a71ddc6e737" (UniqueName: "kubernetes.io/csi/ebs.csi.aws.com^vol-0e6b91392bdce66f3") on node "ip-172-18-5-140.ec2.internal" This volume is not safe to detach, but maxWaitForUnmountDuration 6m0s expired, force detaching
```

Note that the Pod is still in the API server:
```
NAME      READY   STATUS        RESTARTS   AGE
testpod   0/1     Terminating   0          9m26s
```

And the node is healthy:
```
NAME                           STATUS   ROLES    AGE   VERSION
ip-172-18-5-140.ec2.intern

enrichment.problem: The attach-detach controller would force‑detach CSI volumes after a 6‑minute timeout even when the node was healthy. This caused volumes to be detached while still mounted, leading to potential data corruption and stale mount state on the node.
enrichment.affected: Pods with attachable CSI volumes and the nodes they run on; especially scenarios where a pod is deleted but the volume cannot be unmounted quickly.
enrichment.fix: The 6‑minute force‑detach timeout is now applied only to nodes that are unhealthy (node.status.conditions["Ready"] != true). Healthy nodes will no longer have volumes force‑detached after the timeout; the controller will wait for proper unmount before detaching.
enrichment.impact: Prevents data loss and corruption for workloads using CSI volumes, keeping volume mounts consistent on healthy nodes and improving overall storage reliability.

issueContext.title: kubectl discovery dramatically slower on MacOS than Linux
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

We use _a lot_ of CRDs (frequently more than 1,000) in the @crossplane project. This has historically caused a bunch of problems with client-side API discovery, among other things. At the time of writing the latest releases of kubectl use a discovery client rate limiter with a generous QPS and burst (50 qps, 300 qps burst), so client-side rate limiting doesn't become a problem until the API server is serving more than 300 API groups.

Despite rate-limiting no longer coming into effect, we noticed that discovery was very slow - taking 10-20 seconds to complete. After having a few folks at @upbound run a little test (see https://github.com/crossplane/crossplane/issues/2895#issuecomment-1162688419 and following comments) we noticed that discovery specifically seems slow on MacOS - it's _dramatically_ faster on Linux.

Here's discovery happening on Linux with 1,577 CRDs across 343 API groups in around a second:

```shell
$ kubectl --kubeconfig=$HOME/.kube/config.eks version

$ kubectl --kubeconfig=$HOME/.kube/config.eks get crd|wc -l
1577

$ kubectl --kubeconfig=$HOME/.kube/config.eks api-versions|wc -l
343

$ rm -rf ~/.kube/cache

$ time kubectl --kubeconfig=$HOME/.kube/config.eks get nodes
NAME                                            STATUS   ROLES    AGE   VERSION
ip-192-168-103-188.us-west-2.compute.internal   Ready    <none>   8h    v1.22.9-eks-810597c
ip-192-168-63-15.us-west-2.compute.internal     Ready    <none>   8h

enrichment.problem: Kubectl discovery cache updates were slow on macOS, causing discovery of many CRDs (e.g., >1,000) to take 10‑20 seconds, whereas Linux was much faster.

issueContext.title: Kubelet should not report metrics from init containers
issueContext.body:
<!-- Feature requests are unlikely to make progress as an issue.

Instead, please suggest enhancements by engaging with SIGs on slack and mailing lists.

A proposal that works through the design along with the implications of the change can be opened as a KEP:
https://git.k8s.io/enhancements/keps#kubernetes-enhancement-proposals-keps
-->

#### What would you like to be added:
as discussed in issue [#792](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/metrics-server/issues/792) and[#796](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/metrics-server/issues/796) , we get the metrics of terminated container. metric information about terminated pods is expected? If so,  that has changed recently?
#### Why is this needed:
 Kubelet endpoints and CRI metrics protos should report metrics for terminated container should be standardized

enrichment.problem: Kubelet was exposing metrics for containers that had already terminated (including init containers), causing metrics servers to receive and possibly surface stale or irrelevant data.
enrichment.affected: Users relying on kubelet metrics (e.g., Prometheus, metrics‑server, autoscalers) were seeing terminated container data in their dashboards and alerts.
enrichment.fix: Kubelet now filters out metrics from any container that is in a terminated state, ensuring only live container metrics are reported via the metrics endpoint and CRI metrics APIs.
enrichment.impact: Monitoring and autoscaling components that consume kubelet metrics will see more accurate, up‑to‑date data, preventing misleading alerts or scaling decisions based on terminated container metrics.

bugOrRegression.description: UserName check for 'ContainerAdministrator' is now case-insensitive if runAsNonRoot is set to true on Windows.
bugOrRegression.author: marosset

enrichment.problem: On Windows, the kubelet performed a case‑sensitive check for the username 'ContainerAdministrator' when the pod’s securityContext.runAsNonRoot was true. This caused pods that specified the user with a different case (e.g., 'containeradministrator') to be rejected even though the user is effectively the same.
enrichment.affected: Windows workloads that set securityContext.runAsNonRoot=true and specify the ContainerAdministrator user with any case variation.
enrichment.fix: The username validation logic was changed to be case‑insensitive for the ContainerAdministrator account when runAsNonRoot is enabled on Windows, allowing any case variation of the name to be accepted.
enrichment.impact: Pods using Windows containers with runAsNonRoot=true and a ContainerAdministrator user can now start successfully regardless of case, preventing unnecessary pod failures and improving the developer experience on Windows nodes.

bugOrRegression.description: kubeadm: respect user specified image repository when using Kubernetes ci version
bugOrRegression.author: SataQiu

enrichment.problem: kubeadm ignored a user‑specified image repository when initializing a cluster with a Kubernetes CI version, causing images to be pulled from the default registry instead of the intended one.
enrichment.affected: Clusters initialized with kubeadm using a Kubernetes CI version and a custom image repository.
enrichment.fix: kubeadm now honors the imageRepository setting for CI builds, pulling all control‑plane images from the repository specified by the user.
enrichment.impact: Users who rely on custom or mirrored registries for CI images (e.g., air‑gapped environments, private registries) will get the correct images, avoiding unexpected pulls from the public registry and ensuring consistent cluster bootstrapping.

bugOrRegression.description: A bug was fixed where a job sync was not retried in case of a transient ResourceQuota conflict.
bugOrRegression.author: alculquicondor
bugOrRegression.userFacingChange: Fix bug where a job sync is not retried when there is a transient ResourceQuota conflict

enrichment.problem: When a Job's sync operation encountered a transient ResourceQuota conflict, the controller did not retry the sync, causing the Job to remain unscheduled or stuck despite the conflict being temporary.
enrichment.affected: Users running batch workloads (Jobs) that rely on ResourceQuota limits could see jobs stuck in pending state during transient quota conflicts.
enrichment.fix: The Job controller logic now retries the sync operation when a ResourceQuota conflict error is detected, ensuring the Job can proceed once the quota issue resolves.
enrichment.impact: Jobs that previously failed to start due to brief quota conflicts will now be retried automatically, improving reliability of batch workloads and preventing unnecessary manual intervention.

bugOrRegression.description: bug fix in test/e2e/framework  Framework.RecordFlakeIfError
bugOrRegression.author: alingse

enrichment.problem: Framework.RecordFlakeIfError in the e2e testing framework did not correctly record flaky test occurrences, leading to inaccurate test results and potential false failures in CI.
enrichment.affected: Developers and CI systems that run the Kubernetes e2e test suite; flaky test detection was previously unreliable.
enrichment.fix: Implemented proper handling in Framework.RecordFlakeIfError so that errors are correctly logged as flakes, ensuring accurate flake detection and reporting.
enrichment.impact: Improves the reliability of e2e test runs and CI pipelines by correctly distinguishing flaky tests from genuine failures, reducing noise and debugging effort for developers.

bugOrRegression.description: Made usage of key encipherment optional in API validation.
bugOrRegression.author: pacoxu
bugOrRegression.userFacingChange: Modify the signing/approving controller to tolerate either set of usages for kubelet client and serving certificates without key encipherment

enrichment.problem: API validation required the key encipherment usage in kubelet client and serving certificates. Certificates that omitted this usage were rejected, causing kubelet communication and certificate approval failures.
enrichment.affected: Clusters that use kubelet client or serving certificates lacking the key encipherment usage, especially those leveraging external certificate authorities.
enrichment.fix: The signing/approving controller and API validation have been updated to accept certificates that either include or omit the key encipherment usage for kubelet client and serving certificates.
enrichment.impact: Clusters using custom or externally‑generated certificates without key encipherment can now operate without errors, preventing node‑certificate related outages and reducing the need to regenerate certificates.

bugOrRegression.description: Fixed the GCE firewall update when the destination IPs are changing so that firewalls reflect the IP updates of the LBs.
bugOrRegression.author: sugangli
bugOrRegression.userFacingChange: This change fixes the gce firewall update when the destination IPs are changing so that firewalls reflect the IP updates of the LBs.

enrichment.problem: GCE firewall rules were not updated when the destination IP addresses of LoadBalancer services changed, causing stale firewall configurations that could block traffic to the new load balancer IPs.
enrichment.affected: Clusters running on Google Cloud that use Service type LoadBalancer; the GCE cloud-controller-manager responsible for firewall management.
enrichment.fix: The GCE cloud provider logic now detects changes to the load balancer destination IPs and updates the corresponding firewall rules to reflect the new IPs.
enrichment.impact: LoadBalancer services on GCE continue to receive traffic after IP changes, preventing service disruptions and ensuring firewall rules stay in sync with load balancer endpoints.

bugOrRegression.description: kubeadm: enabled the --experimental-watch-progress-notify-interval flag for etcd and set it to 5s. The flag specifies an interval at which etcd sends watch data to the kube-apiserver.
bugOrRegression.author: p0lyn0mial
bugOrRegression.userFacingChange: kubeadm: enable the --experimental-watch-progress-notify-interval flag for etcd and set it to 5s. The flag specifies an interval at which etcd sends watch data to the kube-apiserver.

enrichment.problem: etcd did not send periodic watch progress notifications to the kube-apiserver, which could cause watches to appear stalled or time out, affecting controllers and other watch consumers.
enrichment.affected: Clusters created with kubeadm that run etcd and rely on watch streams (e.g., controllers, operators) may experience delayed or stalled watches without this change.
enrichment.fix: kubeadm now enables the --experimental-watch-progress-notify-interval flag for etcd and sets the interval to 5 seconds, ensuring etcd regularly notifies the kube-apiserver of watch progress.
enrichment.impact: Improves reliability of watch‑based components (e.g., controllers, operators) by reducing watch stalls and timeouts, leading to more responsive cluster behavior.

bugOrRegression.description: Updated max azure data disk count map with new VM types.
bugOrRegression.author: bennerv
bugOrRegression.userFacingChange: update max azure data disk count map with new VM types

enrichment.problem: The internal map of maximum Azure data disk counts did not include newer Azure VM types, which could cause disk provisioning errors or incorrect limits when users tried to attach disks to those VMs.
enrichment.affected: Kubernetes clusters using the Azure cloud provider, particularly those that create Azure PersistentVolumes on the newly added VM types.
enrichment.fix: The map has been updated to add the new Azure VM types along with their correct maximum data disk counts, ensuring the cloud provider reports accurate limits.
enrichment.impact: Users running Kubernetes on Azure with the newly supported VM families can now reliably create and attach the maximum number of data disks supported by those VMs, avoiding pod or node failures due to mismatched limits.

bugOrRegression.description: Windows kubelet plugin Watcher now working as intended.
bugOrRegression.author: claudiubelu

issueContext.title: kubelet: The Plugin Watcher not working as intended on Windows
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

Looking at [1], we can see that the plugin Watcher is traversing the plugin directory, and check whether a new file is a unix socket or not. However, ``mode&os.ModeSocket != 0``, will never be True on Windows. We can also see this in the logs when running the unit test ``TestDevicePluginReRegistrationProbeMode``:

```
I0726 14:24:39.533351    8104 plugin_watcher.go:149] "Ignoring file" path="C:\\Users\\capi\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\device_plugin302605223\\device-plugin.sock" mode="-rw-rw-rw-"
I0726 14:24:39.533351    8104 plugin_watcher.go:149] "Ignoring file" path="C:\\Users\\capi\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\device_plugin302605223\\server.sock" mode="-rw-rw-rw-"
```

Those file should not have been ignored.

Instead of using ``mode&os.ModeSocket != 0``, we should use instead ``util.IsUnixDomainSocket``, which also has a Windows implementation [2].

This issue may also cause the unit tests ``TestPluginRegistration`` and ``TestPluginRegistrationAtKubeletStart`` to flake [3].

[1] https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/7a8f8a32092ede759519f600ca4ac1a319a0bc1d/pkg/kubelet/pluginmanager/pluginwatcher/plugin_watcher.go#L139
[2] https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/7a8f8a32092ede759519f600ca4ac1a319a0bc1d/pkg/kubelet/util/util_windows.go#L140
[3] https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-jenkins/pr-logs/pull/110981/pull-ci-kubernetes-unit-windows/1546592017314746368

### What did you expect to happen?

Instead of using ``mode&os.ModeSocket != 0``, we should use instead ``util.IsUnixDomainSocket``, which also has a Windows implementation [2]. This will result in the plugin Watcher to work as intended.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Run the ``TestDevicePluginReRegistrationProbeMode`` unit test.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Kubernetes version

Kubernetes v1.25, v1.24.

### Cloud provider

N/A

### OS version

Windows Server 2019 or newer.

### Install tools

<details>

enrichment.problem: On Windows, the kubelet plugin watcher incorrectly ignored device plugin socket files because it used a Unix-specific file mode check (mode&os.ModeSocket), which never evaluates true on Windows. This prevented the watcher from detecting new plugins and caused related unit tests to flake.
enrichment.affected: Windows kubelet nodes using device plugins; developers running Windows unit tests for the kubelet.
enrichment.fix: Replaced the Unix-specific mode check with util.IsUnixDomainSocket, which includes a Windows implementation, ensuring socket files are correctly recognized by the plugin watcher.
enrichment.impact: The plugin watcher now correctly discovers and registers device plugins on Windows nodes, restoring expected functionality for workloads that depend on device plugins and stabilizing related unit tests.

issueContext.title: apiserver: Request for a custom resource leads to > 1000% CPU usage increase for more than 10min
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

We observe a high CPU usage of apiserver replicas while other replicas are idling:

```
$ k top po -l role=apiserver
kube-apiserver-786785f6fc-q2fwc               49m          737Mi
kube-apiserver-786785f6fc-r2bxz               50m          690Mi
kube-apiserver-786785f6fc-tbph4               11387m       898Mi
kube-apiserver-786785f6fc-zjfvj               35m          544Mi
```

After investigations we managed to drill down to a custom resource create/update requests that cause this high CPU usage (See the steps to reproduce for more details). It makes sense to mention that the above `k top po` output is from a single Node cluster.

We observe that after such request, the CPU usage does not cool down in seconds or a minute. We see that an apiserver replica is affected by high CPU usage for 10-20min. So it takes 10-20min until the apiserver replica's CPU usage goes down again to values from before the request.

Note also the huge imbalance between the apiserver replica's CPU usage. The replica that get's the requests from the client that operates on the custom resources vs the other 3 replicas that are simply idling wrt CPU usage.



### What did you expect to happen?

I would expect a create request for a custom resource to do not fail with a timeout after 30 seconds.
I would expect such request to do not cause > 1000% CPU usage increase for the concrete apiserver replica for more than 10min.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Example CRD and CR can be found in https://gist.github.com/ialidzhikov/a27fdcea78bd3a0fe726b25c0dfc53c0.

1. Create the `clusterserviceplans.servicecatalog.k8s.io` CRD

   ```
   
2. Try to create a CR:

   ```
   $ k create -f https://gist.githubusercontent.com/ialidzhikov/a

enrichment.problem: Creating large custom resource objects with Server-Side Apply (SSA) on CRDs that have preserveUnknownFields=true caused the apiserver to consume >1000% CPU for many minutes, leading to request timeouts and degraded cluster performance.
enrichment.affected: Users who create or update large custom resources via SSA on CRDs that use preserveUnknownFields (unspecified schemas). The issue manifested as high CPU usage on the kube-apiserver handling those requests.
enrichment.fix: Optimized the apiserver handling of SSA for objects with fully unspecified schemas, reducing CPU work when processing large objects with preserveUnknownFields.
enrichment.impact: API requests for large custom resources now complete quickly without spiking CPU, preventing apiserver overload and improving overall cluster stability and responsiveness.

bugOrRegression.description: Fixed JobTrackingWithFinalizers when a pod succeeds after the job is considered failed, which led to API conflicts that blocked finishing the job.
bugOrRegression.author: alculquicondor
bugOrRegression.userFacingChange: Fix JobTrackingWithFinalizers when a pod succeeds after the job is considered failed, which led to API conflicts that blocked finishing the job.

enrichment.problem: When a pod in a Job succeeded after the Job had already been marked failed, the JobTrackingWithFinalizers logic caused API conflicts that prevented the Job controller from completing the Job termination.
enrichment.affected: Users running Kubernetes Job workloads with finalizers, particularly when a pod can succeed after the Job was marked failed.
enrichment.fix: Adjusted the JobTrackingWithFinalizers implementation to correctly handle a pod succeeding after a failure, eliminating the conflicting API updates and allowing the Job to finish as expected.
enrichment.impact: Jobs that use finalizers will no longer get stuck in a failed state due to API conflicts, ensuring proper job completion and reducing manual intervention.

bugOrRegression.description: Removed the recently re-introduced schedulability predicate ([#109706](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/109706)) as to not have unschedulable nodes removed from load balancers back-end pools.
bugOrRegression.author: alexanderConstantinescu
bugOrRegression.userFacingChange: Remove the recently re-introduced schedulability predicate (by PR: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/109706) as to not have unschedulable nodes removed from load balancers back-end pools.

enrichment.problem: A recently re‑introduced schedulability predicate caused nodes that were marked unschedulable to be automatically removed from cloud provider load balancer back‑end pools, potentially dropping traffic from those nodes.
enrichment.affected: Clusters using cloud provider load balancers (e.g., AWS ELB, GCP LB, Azure LB) where nodes may become unschedulable; the issue affected the scheduler’s node‑selection logic.
enrichment.fix: The predicate introduced in PR #109706 has been removed, so unschedulable nodes are no longer pruned from load balancer back‑end pools.
enrichment.impact: Prevents unintended removal of nodes from load balancer pools, preserving traffic distribution and high‑availability for workloads even when nodes become temporarily unschedulable.

bugOrRegression.description: Fixed memory leak in the job controller related to `JobTrackingWithFinalizers`.
bugOrRegression.author: alculquicondor
bugOrRegression.userFacingChange: Fix memory leak in the job controller related to JobTrackingWithFinalizers

enrichment.problem: The job controller leaked memory when handling Job objects with the JobTrackingWithFinalizers feature enabled, causing the controller manager's memory usage to grow over time.
enrichment.affected: Clusters that run Job resources with finalizers (JobTrackingWithFinalizers). The leak affected the kube-controller-manager's job controller, which could impact any workloads creating such Jobs.
enrichment.fix: The controller manager's job controller code was updated to correctly release resources associated with JobTrackingWithFinalizers, eliminating the memory leak.
enrichment.impact: Stops uncontrolled memory growth in the kube-controller-manager, preventing potential OOM situations and improving cluster stability for workloads that create many Jobs or use finalizers.

feature.description: `CSIMigrationvSphere` feature is now enabled by default.

feature.description: Added container probe duration metrics.
feature.author: jackfrancis
feature.userFacingChange: add container probe duration metrics

issueContext.title: Create a duration metric for probes
issueContext.body:
/kind feature
/sig node

As exec probe timeout [bug was fixed](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/1972), upgrade of k8s may lead to unexpected workload disruptions if the exec probe timeout is not corrected properly. Unfortunately there is no easy way today to guess which timeout should be set for the probe. The suggestion is to introduce a duration metric to allow customers to measure this time.

Likely here where other metrics are defined: /pkg/kubelet/prober/prober_manager.go

KEP: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/1972

/assign @jackfrancis
/cc @matthyx

enrichment.problem: Clusters lacked a metric that reports how long container probes (liveness/readiness/exec) take, making it difficult for operators to choose appropriate probe timeouts and risking unexpected workload disruptions.
enrichment.affected: Any workload that uses container probes (especially exec probes) and the cluster operators who set probe timeout values.
enrichment.fix: Introduced a new Prometheus metric that records the duration of each container probe execution, emitted by the kubelet's probe manager.
enrichment.impact: Operators can now observe real probe latency, tune timeout settings appropriately, and avoid unnecessary pod restarts or failures caused by mis‑configured probe timeouts.

feature.description: Added sum feature to `kubectl top pod`
feature.author: lauchokyip

enrichment.problem: kubectl top pod could only display metrics per pod and lacked a way to see aggregated CPU/memory totals across multiple pods.
enrichment.affected: Users of kubectl who rely on `kubectl top pod` for pod‑level resource metrics.
enrichment.fix: Introduces a sum option to `kubectl top pod`, allowing users to request and view the combined resource usage of selected pods.
enrichment.impact: Provides a quick way for operators to assess total resource consumption of a set of pods without manual summation, improving observability and decision‑making for capacity planning.

feature.description: Pod SecurityContext and PodSecurityPolicy supports slash as sysctl separator.
feature.author: mengjiao-liu

issueContext.title: Regex for validating Sysctl values in deployments might not be correct.
issueContext.body:
#### What happened:
The Regex that validates sysctl values in objects doesn't allow names that contain forward slashes. Sysctl values on network subinterfaces contain these forward slashes.

#### What you expected to happen:
Running:
kubectl create -f ./deployment.yaml

Creates the deployment.

#### How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible):

Create a deployment that brings an additional network interface with subinterface into a pod (using something like Multus). 

Interface will appear as eth2.100

sysctl values for this interface will follow the convention "net.ipv4.conf.eno2/100..."

Attempt to set one of these values in the deployment such as:

spec:
  securityContext:
    sysctls:
    - name: net.ipv4.conf.eno2/100.rp_filter
      value: "0"

It will fail validation, even though it seems like that's the valid name. I wasn't able to escape it.

#### Anything else we need to know?:

#### Environment:
- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`): 1.20.5
- Cloud provider or hardware configuration: On-premise
- OS (e.g: `cat /etc/os-release`): Centos 7
- Kernel (e.g. `uname -a`): 5.5.2-1
- Install tools: kubeadm init
- Network plugin and version (if this is a network-related bug):
- Others:

enrichment.problem: The regex that validates sysctl names in PodSecurityContext and PodSecurityPolicy rejected names containing a forward slash ('/'), preventing workloads from setting sysctl values for network sub‑interfaces (e.g., net.ipv4.conf.eno2/100.rp_filter).
enrichment.affected: Workloads that need to set sysctls on network sub‑interfaces (e.g., pods using multus or custom network interfaces) were unable to create or update due to validation errors.
enrichment.fix: Updated the validation logic to accept '/' as a valid separator in sysctl names for both PodSecurityContext and PodSecurityPolicy, allowing such sysctls to be specified without error.
enrichment.impact: Users can now create Deployments, Pods, etc., that set sysctl values for sub‑interfaces (common with multus or other CNI plugins). This restores expected functionality and avoids unnecessary admission failures.

feature.description: Promoted LocalStorageCapacityIsolationFSQuotaMonitoring to beta.
feature.author: pacoxu
feature.userFacingChange: promote LocalStorageCapacityIsolationFSQuotaMonitoring to beta

enrichment.problem: The LocalStorageCapacityIsolationFSQuotaMonitoring feature was only available as an alpha feature, limiting its stability, default usage, and observability for clusters that need accurate monitoring of local storage capacity isolation via filesystem quotas.
enrichment.affected: Clusters running kubelet with the local storage capacity isolation feature enabled, especially those relying on accurate storage quota monitoring for pods.
enrichment.fix: Promoted the LocalStorageCapacityIsolationFSQuotaMonitoring feature to beta status, making it more stable, enabled by default (or ready for default enablement), and supported for production workloads.
enrichment.impact: Clusters can now reliably monitor and enforce local storage capacity isolation using filesystem quotas, improving node storage health visibility and preventing unexpected storage pressure on workloads.

feature.description: Kubeadm: support experimental JSON/YAML output for `kubeadm upgrade plan` with the `--output` flag.
feature.author: pacoxu
feature.userFacingChange: kubeadm: support experimental JSON/YAML output for "kubeadm upgrade plan" with the "--output" flag

enrichment.problem: kubeadm upgrade plan only produced human‑readable text, making it difficult for automation scripts to parse upgrade information programmatically.
enrichment.affected: Users who run `kubeadm upgrade plan` in scripts or automation workflows that need machine‑readable output.
enrichment.fix: Adds an experimental `--output` flag to `kubeadm upgrade plan` that can emit the plan in JSON or YAML format.
enrichment.impact: Enables reliable integration of upgrade planning into CI/CD pipelines, custom tooling, and monitoring systems, reducing parsing errors and simplifying automation.

feature.description: Feature gate `ProbeTerminationGracePeriod` is enabled by default.
feature.author: kerthcet

enrichment.problem: When a pod is terminated, its liveness and readiness probes were stopped immediately, which could cause false negative health checks and interfere with graceful shutdown logic.
enrichment.affected: All clusters using the default kubelet configuration; any pod that is terminated while having liveness/readiness probes enabled.
enrichment.fix: The ProbeTerminationGracePeriod feature gate is now enabled by default, causing the kubelet to honor the pod's terminationGracePeriodSeconds for probes and keep them running during the graceful termination window.
enrichment.impact: Pods now experience a smoother shutdown with probes remaining active for the configured grace period, reducing premature failures and improving reliability for workloads that rely on graceful termination.

feature.description: kubectl: support multiple resources for kubectl rollout status.
feature.author: pjo256

issueContext.title: kubectl rollout status should support multiple resources
issueContext.body:
<!-- Please use this template while reporting a bug and provide as much info as possible. Not doing so may result in your bug not being addressed in a timely manner. Thanks!-->


**What happened**:
```
deployments/
     a.yml
     b.yml
```

`kubectl rollout status -R -f deployments` fails with `error: rollout status is only supported on individual resources and resource collections - 2 resources were found`.

**What you expected to happen**:

The [docs](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/generated/kubectl/kubectl-commands#-em-status-em-) suggest that `-R` should work for multiple resources in a directory when running `rollout status`. 

`status` should've been applied to all resources under `deployments` following https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/20435. `status` was omitted in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/25110 and I wasn't able to find a discussion regarding this omission in other issues.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:

`kubectl rollout status -R -f deployments`

**Anything else we need to know?**:

**Environment**:
- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`): 1.10.7
- Cloud provider or hardware configuration:
- OS (e.g. from /etc/os-release):
- Kernel (e.g. `uname -a`):
- Install tools:
- Others:

<!-- DO NOT EDIT BELOW THIS LINE -->
/kind bug

enrichment.problem: kubectl rollout status only accepted a single resource; using -R or a directory with multiple resources produced an error stating the command only supports individual resources.
enrichment.affected: Anyone using kubectl rollout status with -R or a manifest directory containing multiple resources (e.g., multiple Deployments) could not obtain status.
enrichment.fix: Implemented support for multiple resources in kubectl rollout status, allowing -R and directory inputs to report rollout status for each resource in the set.
enrichment.impact: Users can now check rollout progress for many Deployments (or other rollout-capable resources) in a single command, matching documentation and reducing manual scripting.

feature.description:
End-to-end testing has been migrated from Ginkgo v1 to v2.

When running test/e2e via the Ginkgo CLI, the v2 CLI must be used and `-timeout=24h` (or some other, suitable value) must be passed because the default timeout was reduced from 24h to 1h. When running it via `go test`, the corresponding `-args` parameter is `-ginkgo.timeout=24h`. To build the CLI in the Kubernetes repo, use `make all WHAT=github.com/onsi/ginkgo/v2/ginkgo`.
Ginkgo V2 doesn't accept go test's `-parallel` flags to parallelize Ginkgo specs, please switch to use `ginkgo -p` or `ginkgo -procs=N` instead.
feature.author: chendave
feature.userFacingChange:
End-to-end testing has been migrated from Ginkgo v1 to v2.

ACTION REQUIRED: When running test/e2e via the Ginkgo CLI, the v2 CLI must be used and `-timeout=24h` (or some other, suitable value) must be passed because the default timeout was reduced from 24h to 1h. When running it via `go test`, the corresponding `-args` parameter is `-ginkgo.timeout=24h`. To build the CLI in the Kubernetes repo, use `make all WHAT=github.com/onsi/ginkgo/v2/ginkgo`.
ACTION REQUIRED: Ginkgo V2 doesn't accept go test's `-parallel` flags to parallelize Ginkgo specs, please switch to use `ginkgo -p` or `ginkgo -procs=N` instead.

issueContext.title: Updating the test framework to ginkgo 2.0
issueContext.body:
### What would you like to be added?

Updating the test framework to ginkgo 2.0 will eventually happen I'm sure and I just wanted to have some notes related to this that people can reference.

### Why is this needed?

Just tracking issues that would be related to any updating of ginkgo from 1.0 to 2.0.
- [ ] Custom reporters deprecated https://onsi.github.io/ginkgo/MIGRATING_TO_V2#removed-custom-reporters
  - [ ] The junit reporter will easily be ported (they have a flag for that)
  - [ ] The progress reporter which makes real-time updates easier will take a little more work but should be fine. I'm happy to take this work when it is needed.

enrichment.problem: The e2e test suite was migrated from Ginkgo v1 to v2, but the default test timeout was reduced from 24h to 1h and Ginkgo v2 no longer respects go test's -parallel flags. This causes tests to time‑out or run serially unless the new CLI and timeout flags are used.
enrichment.affected: Developers, CI systems, and anyone running the Kubernetes e2e test suite.
enrichment.fix: Use the Ginkgo v2 CLI (built with `make all WHAT=github.com/onsi/ginkgo/v2/ginkgo`) and explicitly set a suitable timeout (e.g., `-timeout=24h` or `-ginkgo.timeout=24h` when using `go test`). Replace any `-parallel` go test flags with `ginkgo -p` or `ginkgo -procs=N` to achieve parallelism.
enrichment.impact: Developers and CI pipelines that run Kubernetes e2e tests must update their command lines. Without the changes, tests may prematurely fail or run slower, but there is no impact on production clusters.

feature.description:

The number of pods you want to take down during a `RollingUpdate` is configurable using `maxUnavailable` parameter.

feature.description: Added the `Apply` and `ApplyStatus` methods to the dynamic `ResourceInterface`
feature.author: kevindelgado
feature.userFacingChange: Adds the `Apply` and `ApplyStatus` methods to the dynamic `ResourceInterface`

issueContext.title: Add Apply methods to the dynamic client
issueContext.body:
<!-- Feature requests are unlikely to make progress as an issue.

Instead, please suggest enhancements by engaging with SIGs on slack and mailing lists.

A proposal that works through the design along with the implications of the change can be opened as a KEP:
https://git.k8s.io/enhancements/keps#kubernetes-enhancement-proposals-keps
-->

#### What would you like to be added:
Add `Apply` and `ApplyStatus` methods to the dynamic client [ResourceInterface](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/dynamic/interface.go#L33) 

and an implementation in [client-go/dynamic/simple.go](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/dynamic/simple.go)  that calls the Patch w/ apply type on the unstructured and errors if the user is trying they are trying to apply from a read rather than an extract (e.g. if the metadata has managed fields set).

#### Why is this needed:

This aligns the dynamic client's interface more closely with that of typed clients that already expose Apply methods and makes it more obvious how to perform an apply with a dynamic client (instead of making users have to construct the Patch themselves).

enrichment.problem: The dynamic client’s ResourceInterface lacked native Apply and ApplyStatus methods, forcing users to manually construct server‑side apply PATCHes and handle managed fields themselves.
enrichment.affected: Code that uses the dynamic client (client-go) to create or update resources via server‑side apply. Previously required custom Patch construction.
enrichment.fix: Added Apply and ApplyStatus methods to the dynamic ResourceInterface implementation. These methods invoke a Patch of type Apply on unstructured objects and validate that the object is not sourced from a read‑only representation (e.g., has managedFields set).
enrichment.impact: Developers can now perform server‑side apply with the dynamic client as easily as with typed clients, reducing boilerplate, preventing errors, and aligning the dynamic client’s API with existing client‑go conventions.

feature.description: New `KUBECACHEDIR` environment variable was introduced to override default discovery cache directory which is `$HOME/.kube/cache`.
feature.author: ardaguclu
feature.userFacingChange: Introduce new KUBECACHEDIR environment variable to override default discovery cache directory which is $HOME/.kube/cache

enrichment.problem: kubectl and other client-go tools always used the fixed discovery cache directory at $HOME/.kube/cache, offering no way to relocate it for environments where the home directory is read‑only, shared, or otherwise unsuitable.
enrichment.affected: Users of the kubectl CLI (and any client-go based tools) who need to customize the location of the discovery cache.
enrichment.fix: Introduces the KUBECACHEDIR environment variable; when set, kubectl (and the client-go discovery cache logic) uses its value as the cache directory instead of the default $HOME/.kube/cache.
enrichment.impact: Allows users to control where discovery data is stored, enabling use cases such as CI pipelines, restricted home directories, multi‑user setups, and custom cleanup policies, improving flexibility and reliability of CLI operations.

Applying a pod security label to an exempt namespace should return a warning that the namespace is exempt, and the PSA label won't take effect.

/cc @liggitt

feature.description: Updated base image for Windows pause container images to one built on Windows machines to address limitations of building Windows container images on Linux machines.
feature.author: marosset
feature.userFacingChange: Updating base image for Windows pause container images to one built on Windows machines to address limitations of building Windows container images on Linux machines.

issueContext.title: Cannot modify registry keys during Windows pause image build process
issueContext.body:
### What happened?

The Windows pause images is built using buildkit on Linux hosts and this configuration does not allow for the Windows registry to me modified during the container build process.

When Windows containers are built on Windows host machines part of the build process creates 'delta' registry files when get stored in the layer files. These 'delta' registry hive files are applied to the containers active registry when the containers are created.
Chaning the registry files in the container image layers without having the 'delta' files present will result in the changes NOT being present in the container image.


We have an increasing demand for the ability to modify registry in the pause image on Windows such as 
- Disable some services like DiagTrack that negatively impact performance
- Change behavior of RPCSS so it doesn't hijack RPC port (135) for all containers in the pod



### What did you expect to happen?

Things are working as expected given the current build process.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

There are linux utilities like `chntpw` that can modify Windows registry files that I have used to test this out.
https://gist.github.com/marosset/f32bd81aa11527d8ba2ce8e6a62d4255 
After running the container produced from these files you can see the registry changes made by `chntpw` persisted in the container image but these changes are not present in the container's active registry.

```bash
C:\>reg load HKLM\mounted c:\windows\System32\config\SYSTEM
The operation completed successfully.

C:\>reg query HKLM\mounted\ControlSet001\Services\DiagTrack

HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\mounted\ControlSet001\Services\DiagTrack
    DependOnService    REG_MULTI_SZ    RpcSs
    Description    REG_SZ    @%SystemRoot%\system32\diagtrack.dll,-3002
    DisplayName    REG_SZ    @%SystemRoot%\system32\diagtrack.dll,-3001
    ErrorControl    REG_DWORD    0x1
    FailureActions    REG_BINARY    8051010000000000

enrichment.problem: Windows pause container images were built on Linux using buildkit, which cannot modify the Windows registry during the build. As a result, registry changes (e.g., disabling DiagTrack or altering RPCSS behavior) made in the image layers were not applied to the container's active registry, limiting needed customizations for Windows workloads.
enrichment.affected: Customers running Windows containers that rely on modified pause images, such as those needing to disable DiagTrack or change RPCSS settings.
enrichment.fix: The base image for Windows pause containers is now built on Windows machines. Building on Windows preserves the registry delta files, allowing registry modifications within the pause image to be reflected correctly at runtime.
enrichment.impact: Enables Windows users to customize pause images (disable services, adjust RPC behavior), improving performance and reliability of Windows pods. No functional regressions for other platforms.

feature.description: Kubeadm: enhanced the "patches" functionality to be able to patch kubelet config files containing `v1beta1.KubeletConfiguration`. The new patch target is called `kubeletconfiguration` (e.g. patch file `kubeletconfiguration+json.json`).This makes it possible to apply node specific KubeletConfiguration options during `init`, `join` and `upgrade`, while the main `KubeletConfiguration` that is passed to `init` as part of the `--config` file can still act as the global stored in the cluster `KubeletConfiguration`.
feature.author: neolit123
feature.userFacingChange: kubeadm: enhance the "patches" functionality to be able to patch kubelet config files containing v1beta1.KubeletConfiguration. The new patch target is called "kubeletconfiguration" (e.g. patch file "kubeletconfiguration+json.json"). This makes it possible to apply node specific KubeletConfiguration options during "init", "join" and "upgrade", while the main KubeletConfiguration that is passed to "init" as part of the "--config" file can still act as the global / stored in the cluster KubeletConfiguration.

enrichment.problem: kubeadm could not apply patches to kubelet configuration files that use v1beta1.KubeletConfiguration, limiting the ability to set node‑specific Kubelet settings during cluster init, join, or upgrade.
enrichment.affected: Clusters where administrators need node‑specific Kubelet settings during init, join, or upgrade. Users of kubeadm who rely on the --config file for global KubeletConfiguration will benefit from additional granular control.
enrichment.fix: Added a new patch target "kubeletconfiguration" (e.g., kubeletconfiguration+json.json) to kubeadm's patches functionality, allowing JSON patches to be applied to v1beta1.KubeletConfiguration files. This enables per‑node KubeletConfiguration overrides while keeping a global configuration stored in the cluster.
enrichment.impact: Operators can now customize Kubelet settings on a per‑node basis without affecting the cluster‑wide configuration, simplifying node‑specific tuning during lifecycle operations and reducing the need for manual post‑join configuration edits.

feature.description: Feature gate `CSIMigration` was locked to enabled. `CSIMigration` is GA now. The feature gate will be removed in `v1.27`.
feature.author: Jiawei0227
feature.userFacingChange: Feature gate `CSIMigration` is locked to enabled. CSIMigration is GA now. The feature gate will be removed in 1.27

enrichment.problem: The CSIMigration feature gate, which previously could be toggled, is now permanently enabled (locked) as the feature has reached GA. The gate will be removed in v1.27, so clusters that rely on disabling or configuring the gate may encounter unexpected behavior.
enrichment.affected: Clusters that had CSIMigration disabled or relied on the feature gate for custom migration behavior. All workloads using in‑tree volume plugins that migrate to CSI are impacted.
enrichment.fix: The release locks CSIMigration to enabled, marks it as GA, and schedules removal of the feature gate in v1.27. No user action is required; simply stop configuring the CSIMigration gate.
enrichment.impact: Clusters no longer need to manage the CSIMigration flag, eliminating configuration complexity and ensuring consistent CSI migration behavior across all nodes. The upcoming removal prevents future deprecation warnings and simplifies code paths.

feature.description: Promoted the `CSIMigrationPortworx` feature gate to Beta.
feature.author: trierra
feature.userFacingChange:
These changes promote the CSIMigrationPortworx feature gate to Beta (off by default).

issueContext.title: Allow configuration of etcd healthcheck in kube-apiserver
issueContext.body:
### What would you like to be added?

* Allow configuring separate etcd healthcheck timeouts for kube-apiserver's /readyz and /livez. 
* Allow disabling etcd healthcheck entirely in /livez.

### Why is this needed?

This is needed for more graceful degradation of kube-apiserver's performance when the control plane is overloaded.

Overloaded control plane can result in etcd slowness, and /readyz can be used to redirect traffic from it and allow it to recover. However, with failing /livez, kube-apiserver will soon be restarted by liveness probe anyway.

It might also be useful to stop liveness probe from restarting kube-apiserver at all when etcd is slow. Restarting kube-apiserver is unlikely to resolve problems with etcd, and can introduce extra disruption when kube-apiserver's performance is degraded.

enrichment.problem: kube-apiserver did not allow configuring a separate timeout for the etcd health check performed during the /readyz endpoint, making it hard to tune readiness behavior under load or slow etcd conditions.
enrichment.affected: Clusters running kube-apiserver where etcd latency may cause the /readyz endpoint to fail prematurely; operators who need to tune health‑check timeouts.
enrichment.fix: Adds the `--etcd-ready-timeout` flag to kube-apiserver, letting operators set the timeout for the additional etcd check that runs as part of the readyz probe.
enrichment.impact: Admins can now adjust the readiness probe timeout for etcd, preventing premature unready status or unnecessary restarts when etcd is slow, improving control‑plane stability and graceful degradation under overload.

issueContext.title: Pass secret in NodeExpansion Call for the CSI driver
issueContext.body:
In different use cases we need "secret" passed to the CSI driver to perform NodeExpansion which is missing atm .  One of the very visible use case is that, the expansion on LUKS enabled device, which needs the passphrase in order to resize the device on the node.

One other use case is that, at times we need to check the actual size of the image ( for ex: RBD image size in Ceph Cluster) before proceeding on FS resize to avoid false positive returns on fs resize operation. For that we have to connect to the backend cluster which need secret in the request.

Reference#
CSI spec issue # https://github.com/container-storage-interface/spec/issues/445
CSI spec PR # https://github.com/container-storage-interface/spec/pull/457 

**What happened**:

**What you expected to happen**:

CSI plugin/driver get `NodeExpandSecret` which is same as `ControllerExpandSecret`.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:

**Anything else we need to know?**:

**Environment**:
- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`):
- Cloud provider or hardware configuration:
- OS (e.g: `cat /etc/os-release`):
- Kernel (e.g. `uname -a`):
- Install tools:
- Network plugin and version (if this is a network-related bug):
- Others:

enrichment.problem: CSI drivers did not receive any secret during the NodeExpand RPC, preventing drivers that need credentials (e.g., LUKS encrypted volumes or back‑end size checks) from expanding volumes on the node.
enrichment.affected: Clusters using CSI drivers that require a secret for node expansion (e.g., encrypted volumes, Ceph RBD, etc.) could not expand volumes successfully.
enrichment.fix: Kubernetes now includes a NodeExpandSecret in the CSI driver client request, mirroring the existing ControllerExpandSecret, so drivers can use the provided secret during node‑side expansion.
enrichment.impact: Enables volume expansion for workloads that rely on secrets at the node level, such as encrypted block devices or drivers that must query the storage backend, improving reliability and expanding supported use‑cases.
